extracted.intended_audience: improvisational theatre performers, teachers, and comedy improvisers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or guiding short-form and long-form improvisational comedy performance, focusing on status play, spontaneity, acceptance of offers, narrative construction, and mask/trance character work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status play clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the status play clear (who is up, who is down)? Every encounter is a status transaction (high vs. low status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often comes from clear status differentials. Look for explicit signals of who holds high or low status in an interaction. Tactics: lowering status makes a performer more relatable/sympathetic; raising status creates pomposity that can be punctured for humor. Evaluate whether status is communicated clearly through posture, tone, line choices, and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status reversals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do status reversals occur? (shifts of who is 'up' and who is 'down').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status reversals are inherently funny and create comedic surprise. Check timing and escalation of reversals — are they set up and paid off? Use reversals to change audience expectations; poorly signaled reversals can confuse rather than amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of offers (Yes-and)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the performers accepting offers (yes-and) rather than blocking?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key behaviors: Block = 'no' → kills the scene. Accept = 'yes' → continues the scene. Add = build on what was offered. Anti-pattern: blocking or denying an offer stalls momentum. Positive scoring when performers accept, expand, and add new information that moves the scene forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity / Being obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Are performers spontaneous and 'being obvious' rather than over-thinking or second-guessing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnstone: 'An artist who is inspired is being obvious. He's not making any decisions, he's not weighing one idea against another. He's accepting his first thoughts.' Normal education tends to reduce spontaneity; good improv restores child-like obvious responses. The improviser is 'like a man walking backwards' — reacting to what has just happened rather than planning. Penalize over-thinking, hesitation, and attempts to pre-plan cleverness; reward immediate, obvious choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reincorporation / Callbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Are earlier elements reincorporated into later beats to make the story feel fated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reincorporation (bringing back earlier elements) makes stories feel inevitable and satisfying. The audience loves seeing patterns close; use callbacks and returns of motifs, props, lines, or beats to create narrative payoff. Score positively when earlier details are meaningfully reused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative skills (building inevitable stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the performers building stories that feel inevitable and narratively coherent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative skill involves choosing obvious beats, creating cause-and-effect, and steering scenes toward satisfying conclusions. Avoid second-guessing which kills the sense of magic; favor choices that reveal character and escalate stakes. Evaluate scene arcs, clarity of objective, and how well scenes produce a sense of fate/closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masks and trance / character work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do performers use masks and trance techniques to create distinct characters and character-driven choices?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masks and trance are methods for finding strong, physicalized character impulses. Assess whether mask work produces clear, watchable characters and whether performers sustain trance-based choices consistently. This is more prescriptive/training-oriented than a performance-only checkbox, but it informs character clarity and commitment onstage.
